objective: By the end of this lesson you can list what 14 CFR 61.65 requires for the instrument rating, work out your instrument currency and when you need an IPC, log instrument time and safety pilots correctly, and decide in a given scenario whether you may act as PIC under IFR, including under BasicMed.
why: An instrument rating on your certificate is not the same as being legal or ready to fly in the clouds today. Pilots who are rated but not proficient lose control in IMC, so you need to know both the rules and your own limits.

prereading.what: Instrument rating eligibility, knowledge areas, flight training areas, aeronautical experience and limits on device credit.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 61.65

prereading.what: Takeoff and landing currency, instrument experience (61.57(c)) and the instrument proficiency check (61.57(d)).
prereading.label: 14 CFR 61.57(a)-(d)

prereading.what: Logbook entries, logging PIC time, logging instrument time and approaches, and device time.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 61.51

prereading.what: How an IPC is structured, who may give it, the knowledge and skill portions and recordkeeping.
prereading.label: AC 61-98E, Ch 5, 5-1 to 5-4

prereading.what: BasicMed aircraft and operating limits, safety pilots, and flying IFR under BasicMed.
prereading.label: AC 68-1A, 5-1 to 5-3

prereading.what: The six steps to build, adjust and stick to personal minimums.
prereading.label: RMH Ch 2, 2-1 to 2-5

prereading.what: Vestibular and visual illusions, spatial disorientation and how to cope with it.
prereading.label: IFH Ch 3, 3-5 to 3-9

warmup: Your instrument rating is on your certificate, but you have not flown an approach in seven months. Can you file IFR and fly into the clouds today? If not, what exactly would you need first?

key_terms.def: Six approaches, holding, and intercepting and tracking courses, logged within the 6 calendar months before the month of the flight (61.57(c)).
A whole month. Deadlines run to the last day of the month, not to the date you flew.
A check on the Instrument Rating ACS tasks. The only way back after more than six calendar months out of currency (61.57(d)).
A pilot in the other control seat who watches for traffic while you fly under a view-limiting device (91.109(c)).
A hood, foggles or similar device that blocks the outside view so you fly by instruments alone.
Time flown solely by instruments in real instrument weather (IMC).
Time flown solely by instruments with a view-limiting device, or in a simulator or training device.
An FAA-approved ground trainer. Basic (BATD) or advanced (AATD); credit is limited.
Flying as PIC with a U.S. driver's license, a medical course and a physician's exam instead of an FAA medical, within set limits.
Your own weather, wind and performance limits, stricter than the regulations, based on your experience and proficiency.
Actual skill and judgment to fly the flight well today. More than legal currency.
Not knowing your true attitude or motion because your senses give false signals, common without outside references.

chunks.title: Who can earn the instrument rating

body.p: To apply for an instrument rating you must meet the general rules in [[60:249|14 CFR 61.65(a)]]:

bullets: Hold at least a current private pilot certificate with an airplane rating, or apply for the private certificate at the same time [[60:249|14 CFR 61.65(a)(1)]].
Read, speak, write and understand English [[60:249|14 CFR 61.65(a)(2)]].
Log ground training from an authorized instructor, or finish a home-study course, on the knowledge areas [[60:250|14 CFR 61.65(a)(3)]].
Get an instructor endorsement for the knowledge test, then pass it [[60:250|14 CFR 61.65(a)(4), (a)(7)]].
Log flight training from an authorized instructor, get an endorsement for the practical test, then pass it [[60:250|14 CFR 61.65(a)(5), (a)(6), (a)(8)]].

body.p: Knowledge areas include the IFR regulations, the AIM, the ATC system, IFR navigation and approaches, IFR charts, weather reports and forecasts, critical weather and windshear, aeronautical decision making, and crew resource management [[60:250|14 CFR 61.65(b)]].

Flight training must cover eight areas: preflight preparation, preflight procedures, ATC clearances and procedures, flight by reference to instruments, navigation systems, instrument approach procedures, emergency operations, and postflight procedures [[60:251|14 CFR 61.65(c)]].

callout.text: These are minimums for everyone, whatever your ability [[23:10|IFH vii]]. How much training you actually need depends on how fast you reach a satisfactory level of proficiency, and your instructor is the one who judges that [[23:11|IFH viii]].
Already hold an instrument rating in another category, such as helicopter? You don't take another knowledge test [[60:250|14 CFR 61.65(a)(7)]].

check.q: What is the lowest pilot certificate you must hold (or be getting at the same time) to apply for an instrument-airplane rating?
check.a: A private pilot certificate with an airplane rating [[60:249|14 CFR 61.65(a)(1)]].

body.p: For the instrument-airplane rating you must have logged the following [[60:251|14 CFR 61.65(d)]]:

head: Requirement
Minimum
rows: 50 hours, at least 10 of them in airplanes [[60:251|14 CFR 61.65(d)(1)]]
40 hours, in the 61.65(c) areas of operation [[60:251|14 CFR 61.65(d)(2)]]
Instrument time from an authorized instructor with an instrument-airplane rating
3 hours of instrument training in an airplane within 2 calendar months before the practical test [[60:251|14 CFR 61.65(d)(2)(i)]]
Long IFR cross-country with an instructor
Under IFR on a filed flight plan; 250 NM along airways or ATC-directed routing; an approach at each airport; three different kinds of approaches [[60:251|14 CFR 61.65(d)(2)(ii)]]

callout.text: 50 / 40 / 15 / 3 / 250: 50 XC as PIC, 40 instrument, 15 with an instrument instructor, 3 in the last 2 calendar months, a 250 NM IFR trip [[60:251|14 CFR 61.65(d)]].

body.p: Simulators and training devices count, but only up to a limit:

bullets: Full flight simulator or flight training device, with an instructor: up to 20 hours, or up to 30 hours under a part 142 training center program [[60:252|14 CFR 61.65(h)]].

Aviation training device: up to 10 hours in a basic ATD (BATD) or 20 hours in an advanced ATD (AATD). The device and the training must be FAA-approved, and an instructor must give the time [[60:253|14 CFR 61.65(i)]].
All devices together: no more than 20 hours, except the 30-hour part 142 case [[60:253|14 CFR 61.65(j)]].

callout.text: Doing private and instrument together? You may credit up to 45 hours of cross-country time flown performing PIC duties with an instructor toward the 50 hours [[60:252|14 CFR 61.65(g)]].

check.q: You logged 25 hours in an AATD with an instructor. How many count toward the 40 hours of instrument time?
check.a: 20. AATD credit is capped at 20 hours, and so is total device credit outside part 142 [[60:253|14 CFR 61.65(i), (j)]].

chunks.title: What the rating lets you do, and its limits

body.p: You need the right category, class and instrument rating on your certificate to act as PIC under IFR, or in weather below VFR minimums [[60:191|14 CFR 61.3(e)]].

head: With the rating (and current) you may
Rule
rows: Act as PIC under IFR or in weather below VFR minimums
Fly in Class A airspace (18,000 ft MSL up to FL 600). It is IFR only, with a clearance before you enter
Fly IFR in controlled airspace once you have filed an IFR flight plan and received an ATC clearance
Get special VFR at night in an airplane, if you meet the part 61 instrument rules and the airplane is equipped per 91.205(d)

body.p: Limits that stay with you:

bullets: Currency. Without recent instrument experience you may not act as PIC under IFR or in IMC, even with the rating [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)]].
Your pilot certificate still sets the money rules. A private pilot with an instrument rating still may not carry passengers or property for compensation or hire [[60:307|14 CFR 61.113(a)]].
Category II operations need a separate Category II pilot authorization [[60:191|14 CFR 61.3(f)]].
The rating shows you met minimum standards. It does not make you an all-weather pilot, and it is issued on the assumption you will avoid situations beyond your abilities [[23:11|IFH viii]].

callout.text: As PIC you are directly responsible for, and the final authority as to, the operation of the airplane [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(a)]].

check.q: Does the instrument rating let a private pilot accept pay to fly a passenger in IMC?
check.a: No. The rating does not change private pilot limits on compensation or hire [[60:307|14 CFR 61.113(a)]].

body.p: To act as PIC under IFR, or in weather below VFR minimums, you must have performed and logged these tasks within the 6 calendar months before the month of the flight [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]]:

bullets: Six instrument approaches.
Holding procedures and tasks.
Intercepting and tracking courses with navigation systems.

callout.text: 6-HIT: 6 approaches, Holding, Intercepting and Tracking. The window is the 6 calendar months before the month you fly [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]].

body.p: Do them in actual weather, or in simulated conditions with a view-limiting device [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]]. You may also do them in a full flight simulator, flight training device or aviation training device that represents an airplane, in any mix with flying [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(2)]].

Calendar months keep the math simple. Count back from the month you want to fly. Example: you finished your sixth approach, holding and tracking on March 10. For a September flight the window is March through August, so you are current through September 30. On October 1 you are not [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]].

The tasks add up across the window; they don't have to be on one flight. Each month, check that all six approaches and the holding and tracking still fall inside the window [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]].

callout.text: Instrument currency doesn't replace the other rules. You still need a flight review within 24 calendar months [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(c)]], and to carry passengers, 3 takeoffs and landings in 90 days, to a full stop at night [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)-(b)]].

check.q: You finished your last 6-HIT on January 15. What is the last day you may act as PIC under IFR without more approaches?
check.a: July 31. The window for a July flight is January through June [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]].

chunks.title: Lapsed currency: catching up and the IPC

body.p: Miss the deadline and you are not current: you may not act as PIC under IFR or in IMC [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)]]. For up to six calendar months you can still catch up by flying the 6-HIT tasks: in VMC with a view-limiting device and a safety pilot, in an approved device, or with an instructor [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)-(2)]] [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)]].

Once you have failed to meet the instrument experience for more than six calendar months, only an instrument proficiency check (IPC) restores it [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]]. In the March 10 example: current through September 30, catch-up possible October through March, IPC only from April 1.

head: IPC item
What the rules say
rows: The areas of operation in the Instrument Rating ACS for the rating held [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]]. The ACS rating task table lists the required tasks [[15:32|AC 61-98E 5.3]].

In an airplane, or in a full flight simulator or flight training device that represents an airplane [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(2)]]. An AATD may be used within its letter of authorization; a BATD may not [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.2]].

An examiner, an authorized instructor, certain military or company check pilots, or another person the FAA approves [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(3)]]. An instructor needs an instrument rating on both the pilot and instructor certificates [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.1]].
Part 91 rules, charts, weather, preflight planning, IFR systems and instruments, IFR airworthiness, ATC procedures and angle of attack basics [[15:31|AC 61-98E 5.2.1]] [[15:32|AC 61-98E 5.2.1]]
No failed IPC entry. The instructor logs it as dual instruction given [[15:33|AC 61-98E 5.4.1]].

callout.text: Use the IPC to find weak spots, not just to get a signature. After the check, the instructor should give a full analysis with suggestions for weak areas [[15:32|AC 61-98E 5.4]] [[15:33|AC 61-98E 5.4]].

check.q: Your instrument currency lapsed 8 calendar months ago. Can six hood approaches with a safety pilot fix it?
check.a: No. After more than six calendar months out of currency, only an IPC restores it [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]].

body.p: You must record the training and experience you use for a certificate, rating, flight review or recent experience [[60:227|14 CFR 61.51(a)]]. Each entry needs the date, total time, where you departed and arrived, the aircraft or device type and ID, and the safety pilot's name when 91.109 requires one [[60:227|14 CFR 61.51(b)(1)]]. Also log the conditions: day or night, actual instrument, or simulated instrument [[60:228|14 CFR 61.51(b)(3)]].

head: Situation
What you log
rows: Flying solely by reference to instruments, actual or simulated
The location and type of each approach, and the safety pilot's name if one was required [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(3)]]
Instructor teaching in actual instrument conditions
The instructor may log instrument time too [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(2)]]
An instructor must be present and sign your logbook or training record [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(4)]]
Record the device, the time and the content [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(5)]]
Instructor signs with a description, the lesson length, certificate number and expiration or recent-experience date [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(h)(2)]]

body.p: A summary like Figure 2-2 keeps your IFR picture in one place: IPC date, IFR hours, actual IMC hours and approaches [[30:14|RMH 2-2]].

callout.text: Only time flown solely by instruments is instrument time [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(1)]]. The takeoff and climb before you enter the clouds or put on the view-limiting device don't count.
Show your pilot certificate, medical certificate and logbook when the FAA, the NTSB or a law enforcement officer reasonably asks [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(i)(1)]].

check.q: You flew an RNAV (GPS) approach at a nearby airport under the hood. Which two items must the logbook entry show for currency?
check.a: The location and type of the approach, and the safety pilot's name [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(3)]].

body.p: You may not fly in simulated instrument flight unless [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)]]:

bullets: The other control seat has a safety pilot with at least a private pilot certificate with the right category and class rating, here airplane single-engine land [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]].
The safety pilot can see well forward and to each side, or a competent observer helps [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]].

The airplane has fully working dual controls. A single-engine airplane with a throwover control wheel is allowed if the safety pilot decides the flight is safe and the pilot flying has at least a private certificate [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(3)]].

body.p: The safety pilot is a required pilot flight crewmember, so they need a valid medical certificate [[36:14|AC 68-1A 5.2.2.1]] [[60:189|14 CFR 61.3(c)(1)]]. The rule does not require the safety pilot to hold an instrument rating [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]].

head: Who logs what
Rule
rows: Pilot under the hood: PIC time as sole manipulator of the controls, plus simulated instrument time
Safety pilot: may log PIC only while acting as PIC, because 91.109 makes a second pilot required for that flight
Safety pilot: no instrument time, because they are not flying by instruments

callout.text: Decide who is PIC before engine start. Under IFR the PIC must be instrument rated and current [[60:191|14 CFR 61.3(e)]] [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)]]. Brief the control handoff too: one pilot says it, the other accepts it, the first confirms it [[15:9|AC 61-98E 2.1.1]].

check.q: Your friend is a private pilot with no instrument rating and a current medical. Can she be your safety pilot in VMC?
check.a: Yes. 91.109(c) asks for a private certificate with airplane single-engine land and good vision [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)]]. As a required crewmember she needs her medical [[36:14|AC 68-1A 5.2.2.1]].

body.p: BasicMed lets a private pilot act as PIC without an FAA medical certificate, using a valid U.S. driver's license, if the pilot meets 61.23(c)(3) and the flight stays within set limits [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)]].

head: You must
Rule
rows: Have held an FAA medical certificate at some time after July 14, 2006. The latest may be expired, but not suspended or revoked
Complete the BasicMed medical education course within the past 24 calendar months
Get a comprehensive medical exam from a state-licensed physician within the past 48 calendar months
Keep the exam checklist and the course completion certificate in your logbook

head: Limit
Under BasicMed [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(1)-(2)]]
rows: Authorized for 7 occupants or fewer, max takeoff weight 12,500 lb or less
Inside the United States, unless the other country authorizes it

body.p: **IFR is allowed.** You may fly IFR and in IMC under BasicMed. BasicMed does not change the need for an instrument rating and instrument currency, and the airplane must still be approved for IFR [[36:14|AC 68-1A 5.2.3]].

bullets: The 18,000 ft limit keeps you out of Class A airspace [[33:179|AIM 3-2-2]]. If ice or thunderstorms on the route could force a climb above 18,000 ft, the FAA considers starting the flight contrary to BasicMed [[36:15|AC 68-1A 5.2.4.2]].
A safety pilot may use BasicMed only while acting as PIC. Otherwise the safety pilot needs a medical certificate [[36:14|AC 68-1A 5.2.2.1]].
You may receive instrument training from an instructor while operating under BasicMed [[36:14|AC 68-1A 5.2.2.2]].

callout.text: AC 68-1A (2017) still lists 6 occupants, 6,000 lb and 5 passengers [[36:13|AC 68-1A 5.1.1, 5.2.1]]. The current regulation says 7 occupants, 12,500 lb and 6 passengers [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(1)]]. Use the regulation.

check.q: On BasicMed, ice is forecast from 8,000 to 16,000 ft with tops at 20,000 ft. Your plan is to climb on top. OK?
check.a: No. You may not fly above 18,000 ft MSL on BasicMed, and starting a flight that may need it is contrary to BasicMed [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(2)]] [[36:15|AC 68-1A 5.2.4.2]].

body.p: Currency is the legal minimum. Proficiency is being able to fly this flight well today. The rating only certifies that you met the minimum experience and showed acceptable skill and judgment [[23:11|IFH viii]].

head: Currency
Proficiency
rows: Set by regulation: 6-HIT in 6 calendar months [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)]]
Set by you: the knowledge, skill and judgment the flight needs [[15:9|AC 61-98E 2.1.2]]
An honest self-check of your recent flights, ideally with an instructor [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]
Can be met in smooth VMC under a hood
Needs practice in the conditions you will fly, including manual flying with automation failed [[15:13|AC 61-98E 2.2.3]]

body.p: Spatial disorientation and loss of control in IMC catch non-instrument pilots. They also catch pilots who are instrument rated but not instrument proficient [[15:12|AC 61-98E 2.1.5]]. Loss of control usually happens when pilots lack proficiency [[15:9|AC 61-98E 2.1.2]].
Build a personal currency program that aims above the 14 CFR minimums [[15:7|AC 61-98E 1.9.1]]:

bullets: Fly extra approaches as part of normal trips instead of separate currency flights [[15:7|AC 61-98E 1.9.1]].
Use FAASTeam WINGS courses and safety seminars [[15:7|AC 61-98E 1.9.2]].
Hand-fly at times to keep manual skills sharp [[15:13|AC 61-98E 2.2.2]].
Fly night and VFR traffic-area trips too; they build instrument skill and divided attention [[23:313|IFH 10-22]].

callout.text: Legal is not the same as smart. Know the difference between what the rules allow and what is safe for your experience and proficiency [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]].

check.q: You flew six hood approaches, holding and tracking in calm VMC five months ago, nothing since. Today the ceiling is 400 ft and gusty. Legal? Smart?
check.a: Legal, but you are not proficient for these conditions. Practice with an instructor first or wait [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)]] [[15:9|AC 61-98E 2.1.2]].

body.p: Regulations don't cover every situation or guarantee safety. Personal minimums are limits you set that are stricter than the rules, based on your experience and proficiency [[30:13|RMH 2-1]].

The RMH builds minimums in six steps: review the weather categories, assess your experience and comfort level, add wind, turbulence and performance limits, assemble a baseline, adjust for the day, and stick to the plan [[30:13|RMH 2-1]] [[30:16|RMH 2-4]] [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].
In this sample the pilot's IFR minimums are 800 ft and 1 mile by day, 999 ft and 3 miles at night. The LIFR boxes are blank because the pilot decided to avoid those conditions [[30:15|RMH 2-3]].

Then adjust the baseline for the day. If more than one factor applies, adjust for each one. The RMH example: a night trip to an unfamiliar airport after a full workday raises the minimums by 1,000 ft of ceiling, 1 mile of visibility and 1,000 ft of runway [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

callout.text: Three cautions: don't lower your minimums to complete a specific flight; change one variable at a time; and see an instructor before a big change [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

body.p: RMH case study: a pilot worried about her instrument proficiency added 500 ft to her minimums for the approach and chose an alternate she could reach with her fuel [[30:41|RMH 5-3]].

check.q: Why write your personal minimums down before you need them?
check.a: So you make go, no-go and divert decisions by the numbers instead of under pressure. A written set also helps explain the decision to passengers [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

chunks.title: Risk: fitness for flight and your senses in IMC

body.p: Do a physical self-check before every flight [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]. In IMC it matters even more: illness, medication, alcohol, fatigue, sleep loss and mild hypoxia all make spatial disorientation more likely [[23:75|IFH 3-8]] [[23:76|IFH 3-9]].

head: IMSAFE
Ask yourself [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]]
rows: Am I taking medicine that might affect my judgment or make me drowsy?
Am I under pressure from work, money, health or family?
Have I been drinking within 8 hours? Within 24 hours?
Am I tired and not well rested?

bullets: No acting as a crewmember within 8 hours of a drink, while under the influence, at 0.04 or more, or on a drug that affects your faculties against safety [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)]].
Don't act as PIC if you know of a medical condition that would make you fail your medical standard, or under BasicMed, that would keep you from flying safely [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53(a)-(c)]].
New medicine: wait at least 48 hours after the first dose. For a medicine with side effects such as drowsiness, wait at least five dosing intervals [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

body.p: Your inner ear can lie. When a turn starts, moving fluid gives the feeling of turning. In a steady turn the fluid catches up and you feel no turn. When you level out, you feel a turn the other way [[23:72|IFH 3-5]].

That is how the leans start: you roll back into the turn or lean in your seat to match a false sense of bank [[23:72|IFH 3-5]]. Skids, slips and uncoordinated turns all feel alike in the seat [[23:74|IFH 3-7]].

callout.text: The defense: get proficient on instruments and rely on them. Trust the instruments and disregard your body's sensations. Avoid sudden head movements, and be rested and fed before flying in low visibility [[23:75|IFH 3-8]] [[23:76|IFH 3-9]].

check.q: You have been in a steady, coordinated turn in the clouds for 30 seconds. What does your inner ear tell you?
check.a: That you are not turning. The fluid has caught up with the canal, so there is no sensation of turning [[23:72|IFH 3-5]].

body.p: Learn the airplane's systems, limits and procedures before you fly it. Pay special attention to the flight instruments, avionics and navigation equipment, legacy or modern [[57:9|AC 90-109A 6c(1)]]. Get a thorough checkout from an instructor, preferably one with recent experience in that make and model [[57:10|AC 90-109A 6c(2)]].

These two PFDs come from different makers [[23:123|IFH 5-28]]. Pilots must be fully trained on the avionics they use, and still be able to fly by hand if the automation fails [[57:52|AC 90-109A App 10, 1h]]. For automated systems the FAA strongly recommends an evaluation by an instructor experienced with that equipment [[15:13|AC 61-98E 2.2.1]].

head: Hazard
Mitigation
rows: Automation bias: trusting the system more than yourself, "set and go" [[15:13|AC 61-98E 2.2.2]]
Actively manage the automation, cross-check systems, and hand-fly at times [[15:13|AC 61-98E 2.2.2]]
Know how to isolate the failed part and fly the airplane by hand [[15:13|AC 61-98E 2.2.3]]
Raise your personal minimums for that airplane [[30:39|RMH 5-1]] [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]
Build up slowly, and limit who flies with you until you are familiar, except for instruction [[57:6|AC 90-109A 6a(3)(e)]] [[57:7|AC 90-109A 6a(3)(h)]]

callout.text: Moving to a slower airplane is a transition too. Headwinds hurt more, turbulence feels worse and the avionics may be less capable [[57:52|AC 90-109A App 10, 2]].

check.q: You trained on a glass panel and want to rent an airplane with a different panel for an IFR trip. What should you do first?
check.a: Get a thorough checkout from an instructor experienced in that airplane and its avionics [[57:10|AC 90-109A 6c(2)]] [[15:13|AC 61-98E 2.2.1]], and raise your personal minimums until you are familiar [[30:39|RMH 5-1]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: can I be PIC under IFR today?

body.p: Work through this list when the examiner gives you a scenario, and before every IFR flight. Name the rule for each step.

bullets: 1. Documents: pilot certificate and photo ID [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)]], and a medical certificate [[60:189|14 CFR 61.3(c)]] or BasicMed records in your logbook [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(3)]].
2. Ratings: airplane single-engine land, plus the instrument-airplane rating [[60:191|14 CFR 61.3(e)]].
3. Flight review within 24 calendar months. A practical test for a rating, such as your instrument checkride, also counts [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(c)-(d)]].
4. Instrument currency: 6-HIT within the 6 calendar months before this month; if lapsed more than six calendar months, an IPC [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)]] [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)]].
5. Passengers: 3 takeoffs and landings in 90 days, to a full stop at night [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)-(b)]].
6. BasicMed? Check occupants, weight, passengers, altitude and speed [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)]].
7. Fit to fly: IMSAFE, alcohol and drugs, medical deficiency [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]] [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)]] [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53]].
8. IFR preflight action: weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements, alternatives, and known ATC delays [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(a)]].
9. File an IFR flight plan and get an ATC clearance before flying IFR in controlled airspace [[60:471|14 CFR 91.173]].
10. Compare the weather with your personal minimums, adjusted for today [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

head: ACS skill
Standard
rows: Apply the requirements to act as PIC under IFR in a scenario given by the evaluator (ACS IR.I.A.S1)

callout.text: Answer with the reason, not just yes or no: "Not current: my last approaches were in April, so the November window is May through October [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]]."

check.q: Your last flight review was 25 calendar months ago, and you flew a full 6-HIT last month. Can you act as PIC under IFR?
check.a: No. Without a flight review (or a qualifying practical test) in the last 24 calendar months you may not act as PIC at all [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(c)]].

f1.caption: Figure 2-4. A sample pilot experience and comfort level assessment for IFR and LIFR.
f1.alt: Table titled Experience and Comfort Level Assessment, IFR and LIFR. IFR column (red): ceiling 500 to 999, day 800, night 999; visibility 1 to 3 miles, day 1 mile, night 3 miles. LIFR column (pink): ceiling below 500 and visibility below 1 mile, with the day and night boxes left blank.

f2.caption: Figure 2-9. Examples of additional safety margins from baseline personal minimums.
f2.alt: Four colored rows. Pilot: illness, medication, stress, fatigue or lack of currency. Aircraft: an unfamiliar airplane or unfamiliar avionics. enVironment: unfamiliar airports, airspace or terrain. External Pressures: must-meet deadlines and passenger pressure. Right column of margins: add at least 500 ft to ceiling, at least 1/2 mile to visibility, at least 500 ft to runway length, and subtract at least 5 knots from winds.

f3.caption: Figure 2-2. Certification, training, and experience summary.
f3.alt: Green form with blank boxes for certificate level, ratings and endorsements; a training summary with flight review, instrument proficiency check, time since checkout in up to three aircraft and variation in equipment; total flying time and years; and recent experience for the last 12 months including hours, landings, night hours, IFR hours, IMC hours (actual conditions) and approaches (actual or simulated).

f4.caption: Figure 3-5. Angular acceleration.
f4.alt: Four drawings of a semicircular canal with endolymph fluid, cupola and tube labeled: no turning gives no sensation; at the start of a turn the moving fluid bends the hairs and you sense turning; in a constant rate turn the fluid catches up and there is no sensation; when the turn stops the fluid bends the hairs the other way and you sense a turn in the opposite direction.

f5.caption: Figure 3-8. Sensations from centrifugal force.
f5.alt: Six front views of an airplane with a seated pilot and a red arrow for the felt force: level, coordinated turn and pull out all push straight down into the seat; level skid, forward slip and uncoordinated turn all push the pilot sideways. Caption in the figure: skid, slip and uncoordinated turns feel alike.

f6.caption: Figure 5-45. Two primary flight displays (Avidyne on the left and Garmin on the right).
f6.alt: Two glass flight displays side by side, each with an attitude indicator on a blue and brown background, an airspeed tape on the left and an altitude tape on the right. The left unit has soft keys down both sides and a moving heading arc below; the right unit has knobs for NAV, COM, heading, altitude and FMS, frequency boxes along the top and a heading circle with a VOR course below.

scenario.title: A November trip on BasicMed in a new-to-you airplane
scenario.setup: It is November 14. You are an instrument-rated private pilot flying under BasicMed. Your last 6-HIT was logged on April 20, and your flight review was 14 months ago. You plan an IFR trip with two friends in a club airplane whose glass panel you have never used. The destination forecast is a 700 ft ceiling; your written day IFR minimum is 800 ft. You slept 5 hours and took a cold medicine you had never tried before last night. A friend who also flies on BasicMed offers to be your safety pilot for some approaches on the way.

questions.a: No. The window for a November flight is May through October, so your April tasks are outside it. You may not act as PIC under IFR or in IMC [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]]. You have been out less than six calendar months, so you can still make up the 6-HIT without an IPC [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]].

questions.q: Can your BasicMed friend be your safety pilot while you are PIC?
questions.a: No. A safety pilot is a required crewmember. BasicMed covers her only if she is acting as PIC; otherwise she needs a medical certificate [[36:14|AC 68-1A 5.2.2.1]]. And until your 6-HIT is done and logged, neither of you can let you act as PIC under IFR [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)]].

questions.q: Suppose you were current. What do your personal minimums say about the 700 ft forecast?
questions.a: No-go. 700 ft is already below your 800 ft baseline. Illness or medication, fatigue and unfamiliar avionics are each reasons to add margin, not lower it [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]. Never lower your minimums to complete a specific flight [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

questions.q: What about last night's cold medicine?
questions.a: For a new medicine, wait at least 48 hours after the first dose [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]. You may not fly on a drug that affects your faculties against safety [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(3)]], and illness and medication raise the risk of spatial disorientation [[23:75|IFH 3-8]] [[23:76|IFH 3-9]].

questions.q: What should you do about the unfamiliar glass panel before flying it IFR?
questions.a: Get a thorough checkout from an instructor with recent experience in that make and model [[57:10|AC 90-109A 6c(2)]], learn to fly it by hand when automation fails [[15:13|AC 61-98E 2.2.3]], and raise your personal minimums for that airplane [[30:39|RMH 5-1]].

questions.q: Does BasicMed itself stop you from flying this trip IFR?
questions.a: No. BasicMed allows IFR and IMC if you are rated and current and the airplane is approved for IFR [[36:14|AC 68-1A 5.2.3]], within the limits of 6 passengers, 18,000 ft MSL and 250 knots [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)]].

skills.do: Given the evaluator's scenario, decide whether you may act as PIC under IFR and back it up with the rules: certificate and photo ID, medical or BasicMed, instrument rating, flight review, 61.57(c) currency or an IPC, passenger currency, fitness, IFR preflight action, and flight plan and clearance (ACS IR.I.A.S1).
skills.practice: Run the 10-step list in this lesson against your own logbook before every IFR flight. Have your instructor make up logbook pages with different dates for you to judge, including lapsed currency [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)]] [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)]] and an old flight review [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(c)]].

quiz.q: How much cross-country time as PIC must you log for the instrument-airplane rating?
quiz.why: 50 hours of cross-country PIC time, 10 of it in airplanes [[60:251|14 CFR 61.65(d)(1)]]. 40 hours is the instrument time requirement.

quiz.q: What must the required IFR cross-country with an instructor include?
options: 150 NM, landings at three airports, one ILS
250 NM, an approach at each airport, three different kinds of approaches
250 NM, a full-stop landing at each airport, two GPS approaches
100 NM, one approach, flown under VFR
quiz.why: It is flown under IFR on a filed flight plan: 250 NM along airways or ATC-directed routing, an approach at each airport, and three different kinds of approaches [[60:251|14 CFR 61.65(d)(2)(ii)]].

quiz.q: Which tasks keep you instrument current under 61.57(c)?
options: Six approaches and three full-stop landings
Six approaches, holding, and intercepting and tracking courses
quiz.why: Six approaches, holding procedures and tasks, and intercepting and tracking courses with navigation systems [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]].

quiz.q: What is the minimum certificate a safety pilot needs in a single-engine airplane?
options: Private pilot certificate with airplane single-engine land
Private pilot certificate with an instrument rating
Flight instructor certificate with an instrument rating
quiz.why: 91.109(c)(1) asks for at least a private certificate with the right category and class rating. No instrument rating is required [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]].

quiz.q: To use simulator or ATD time for instrument currency, what must you record?
options: The device, the time and the content
An instructor's signature and certificate number
The device's FAA approval letter number
quiz.why: For recency, keep a logbook or training record that shows the device, time and content [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(5)]]. An instructor's signature is needed for device time toward a rating [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(4)]].

quiz.q: Under BasicMed, what is the highest altitude you may fly?
quiz.why: BasicMed flights may not be carried out above 18,000 ft MSL [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(2)(i)]].

quiz.q: Can a pilot operating under BasicMed fly IFR in IMC?
options: Yes, if instrument rated and current, in an airplane approved for IFR
Yes, but only in day IMC
Only with a second pilot on board
quiz.why: BasicMed allows IFR and IMC. It does not remove the need for an instrument rating, instrument currency or an IFR-approved airplane [[36:14|AC 68-1A 5.2.3]].

quiz.q: Which is one of the RMH cautions about personal minimums?
options: Lower them when the trip is important
Don't adjust them to complete a specific flight
Set them equal to the published approach minimums
quiz.why: Don't adjust minimums to complete a specific flight, change one variable at a time, and see an instructor before a big change [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

quiz.q: In a long, steady, coordinated turn in IMC, what does your inner ear sense?
options: A steady turn in the right direction
A turn in the opposite direction
quiz.why: In a constant rate turn the fluid catches up with the canal, so you feel no turn. You feel the opposite turn when you roll out [[23:72|IFH 3-5]].

takeaways: 61.65: private certificate, knowledge test, 50 XC as PIC, 40 instrument (15 with an instructor), 3 within 2 calendar months, and a 250 NM IFR trip.
Currency is 6-HIT in the 6 calendar months before the month of flight. Lapsed more than six calendar months: IPC only.
Log approach type and location, and the safety pilot's name. Only flight solely by instruments is instrument time.
A safety pilot needs a private certificate with airplane single-engine land and a medical (BasicMed only if acting as PIC).
BasicMed allows IFR, but not above 18,000 ft MSL, over 250 knots or over 6 passengers.
Legal is not proficient. Set written personal minimums, add margin for illness, fatigue and unfamiliar airplanes, and stick to them.
cfi_notes: IFH Introduction (p. viii) says the currency tasks are done "within the preceding 6 months," refers to the instrument PTS, and says a "qualified instrument flight instructor" gives the IPC. Current 61.57(c) and (d) use 6 calendar months, the ACS, and a list of who may give an IPC. Teach the regulation.
IFH 10-22 says the recency requirements are in "Part 91." They are in 14 CFR 61.57(c). Point this out.

AC 68-1A (2017) is out of date: it shows 6 occupants, 6,000 lb and 5 passengers, and its 5.2.4.1 describes a compensation limit under 61.113(i)(2)(i) that is not in the 14 CFR text in our files (as of 10/08/2026). Teach the regulation and check the eCFR before each checkride season.
Drill calendar-month math with many dates: last current day, catch-up period, and the first day an IPC is required. Common error: counting six months from the date instead of by whole months.

Common errors: thinking the safety pilot needs an instrument rating, forgetting the safety pilot needs a medical, and leaving the safety pilot's name and the approach type and location out of the logbook.
Examiners often probe who is PIC and who logs what with a safety pilot, BasicMed under IFR (the 18,000 ft limit and safety pilots), and 61.65 device-credit limits.
RMH Figure 2-9 is easy to read row by row. The RMH text says to adjust for each factor that applies; its example with two factors adds 1,000 ft, 1 mile and 1,000 ft of runway. Teach from the text.
Use the scenario to show the difference between legal and proficient, and have the student say their written minimums out loud.
gaps: FAA legal interpretations on when a safety pilot may act as and log PIC, and on logging approaches (InFO 15012), are not in the uploaded sources; the lesson uses the 14 CFR 61.51 text only.
AC 61-65 sample endorsement wording for the knowledge test, practical test and IPC is not in the sources.
61.57(e) part 121/125/135 exceptions and the glider and helicopter instrument rules are left out (single-engine airplane lesson).
Multiengine IPC and multiengine instructor requirements (AC 61-98E 5.1.1) are not taught; this lesson is single-engine land only.
Specific avionics and autopilot procedures for the training airplane come from its POH/AFM and supplements, not these sources.
Part 68 itself (course and exam content) is only summarized through 61.23(c)(3) and AC 68-1A.

Through September 30: current, you may act as PIC under IFR
October 1: not current, no PIC under IFR or in IMC
October through March: make up the 6-HIT with a safety pilot, device or instructor
April 1: out of currency for more than six calendar months

activities.title: True or false: safety pilots, minimums and your senses
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: A safety pilot must hold an instrument rating.
cards.why: No. A private certificate with the right category and class rating is enough [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]].

cards.s: Practicing hood work in VMC under VFR does not require you to be instrument current.
cards.why: 61.57(c) applies to acting as PIC under IFR or in weather below VFR minimums [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)]]. You still need a safety pilot [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)]].

cards.s: Fatigue, illness and medication make spatial disorientation more likely.
cards.why: Yes. Illness, medication, alcohol, fatigue, sleep loss and mild hypoxia increase susceptibility [[23:75|IFH 3-8]] [[23:76|IFH 3-9]].

cards.s: In a long, steady turn in IMC, your inner ear keeps telling you that you are turning.
cards.why: No. Once the fluid catches up, you feel no turn at all [[23:72|IFH 3-5]].

cards.s: If a trip is important, it's fine to lower your personal minimums that morning.
cards.why: No. Don't adjust minimums to complete a specific flight; do it when you have time to think honestly [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

cards.s: Instrument-rated pilots who are not proficient are also at risk of losing control in IMC.
cards.why: Yes. Rated but not proficient pilots are also susceptible to spatial disorientation and loss of control [[15:12|AC 61-98E 2.1.5]].

final_quiz.q: You completed your last 6-HIT on February 3. What is the last day you may act as PIC under IFR without doing more?
final_quiz.why: The window for an August flight is February through July, so you are current through August 31 [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: Your last 6-HIT was on June 12, 2026, and you have done nothing since. From what date is an IPC the only way to get current again?
final_quiz.why: You are current through December 31, 2026, then out January through June 2027. On July 1, 2027 you have been out more than six calendar months, so only an IPC works [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]] [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: You logged 2 approaches in April, 2 in June and 2 in August, plus holding and tracking in August. Through what month are you current?
final_quiz.why: October's window is April through September, which holds all six. November's window starts in May, so the two April approaches drop out [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: Outside part 142 you logged 28 hours in a flight training device and 6 hours in an AATD, all with an instructor. How many device hours count toward the 40?
final_quiz.why: Without part 142, the most you may credit from all devices together is 20 hours [[60:253|14 CFR 61.65(j)]] [[60:252|14 CFR 61.65(h)(2)]].

final_quiz.q: You fly under the hood in VMC while your friend acts as safety pilot. Who may log simulated instrument time?
options: Only you, the pilot flying by instruments
final_quiz.why: Instrument time is logged only by the person operating the airplane solely by reference to instruments, actual or simulated [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: Your friend flies on BasicMed and has no current medical certificate. Can she serve as your safety pilot while you are PIC?
options: Yes, BasicMed covers any crew duty
Yes, if she holds an instrument rating
Only on an IFR flight plan
No, BasicMed covers a safety pilot only while acting as PIC
final_quiz.why: A safety pilot is a required pilot flightcrew member. BasicMed privileges extend only to the person acting as PIC [[36:14|AC 68-1A 5.2.2.1]].

final_quiz.q: Which IFR flight is within the BasicMed limits?
options: A 7-seat, 4,000 lb single with 6 passengers at 11,000 ft and 180 knots indicated
The same airplane cruising at FL 190
A 6-seat turboprop cruising at 270 knots indicated
final_quiz.why: BasicMed allows up to 7 occupants, 12,500 lb, 6 passengers, 18,000 ft MSL and 250 knots indicated [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(1)-(2)]].

final_quiz.q: You are instrument rated and current, in an airplane equipped per 91.205(d). At night the airport is below VFR minimums. May you request special VFR?
options: No, special VFR is never allowed at night
Yes, because you meet the instrument requirements and the airplane is IFR-equipped
Only if you hold a commercial certificate
final_quiz.why: In an airplane, night special VFR needs a pilot who meets the part 61 instrument rules and an airplane equipped per 91.205(d) [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)(4)]].

final_quiz.q: Who may give you an IPC in a single-engine airplane?
options: An authorized instructor with instrument ratings on both pilot and instructor certificates
Any flight instructor, with or without an instrument rating
Any instrument-rated private pilot acting as safety pilot
final_quiz.why: 61.57(d)(3) lists examiners and authorized instructors, among others [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(3)]]. The instructor needs an instrument rating on both certificates [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.1]].

final_quiz.q: Your baseline night IFR minimums are 999 ft and 3 miles. Tonight you fly to an unfamiliar airport after a full workday. Using the RMH example, about what are tonight's minimums?
final_quiz.why: The RMH example for this trip adds 1,000 ft to the ceiling and 1 mile to visibility: 999 + 1,000 is about 2,000 ft, and 3 + 1 = 4 miles [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

final_quiz.q: Your last drink was at 0100. Under the 8-hour rule in 91.17, what is the earliest you may act as a crewmember?
final_quiz.why: No crew duty within 8 hours after drinking: 0100 + 8 hours = 0900. You also must not be under the influence or at 0.04 or more [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)]].

final_quiz.q: You have used a medicine before without trouble, but it can cause drowsiness and is dosed every 6 hours. Using the PHAK rule, how long should you wait after a dose before flying?
final_quiz.why: Wait at least five maximal dosing intervals: 5 x 6 hours = 30 hours [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

final_quiz.q: Which habit best guards against automation bias in a glass-panel airplane?
options: Engage the autopilot right after takeoff and let it fly
Use only the moving map for position
Turn off the PFD and fly the backup instruments only
Actively manage the automation, cross-check systems and hand-fly at times
final_quiz.why: The FAA recommends active automation management, cross-checking data, and hand-flying at times to keep manual skills [[15:13|AC 61-98E 2.2.2]].

final_quiz.q: You passed your instrument practical test 20 calendar months ago and have had no flight review since. Do you need one before acting as PIC this month?
options: Yes, the instrument checkride never counts
Yes, a flight review is due every 12 calendar months for IFR
Only if you will carry passengers
No, a practical test for a rating within 24 calendar months counts
final_quiz.why: A practical test for a rating, passed within the 24 calendar months, replaces the flight review [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(d)(1)]].
